name: Cloud Storage
oneLiner: Unified object storage — the data-lake foundation across Google Cloud.
whatItIs: Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's object store: files ("objects") live in "buckets" and are fetched by name over HTTPS. Like all object stores it is not a filesystem and not a database — objects are immutable blobs, and the slashes in a name are just naming, not real folders. It is the cheap, durable, effectively-unlimited floor that the rest of GCP analytics stands on: raw data lands here, Dataflow and Dataproc process it, and BigQuery loads from or queries directly against it. If you learn one GCP storage service, learn this one.

inPractice.narrative: A team streams app and event data into a Cloud Storage 'raw' bucket — the lake's front door. A Dataflow or Dataproc job cleans and reshapes it into date-partitioned Parquet in a 'curated' bucket. BigQuery then either loads that data or queries it in place as external/BigLake tables, and Looker dashboards read from BigQuery. Cloud Storage appears at both ends — raw landing and curated output — and stays the neutral hand-off point between every tool.

coreConcepts.detail: A bucket is a globally-unique name tied to a location (region, dual-region or multi-region); the object key is the full path within it. As with S3, 'folders' are just key prefixes.

Region (one place, lowest latency/cost), dual-region (two set regions, low-latency HA) or multi-region (a broad geography, highest availability). Analytics workloads usually co-locate the bucket with BigQuery/compute.

Standard (hot), Nearline (~monthly access), Coldline (~quarterly), Archive (rarely). Same API and millisecond access across all classes — colder ones just cost more to read and have minimum storage durations.
GCS is strongly consistent for reads-after-writes and for bucket/object listing — no stale-read caveats to design around.
Autoclass moves objects between classes automatically based on access; lifecycle rules can transition or delete objects by age. Both keep cold data cheap without manual work.
The modern default: permissions via IAM at the bucket level instead of per-object ACLs — simpler and easier to reason about securely.

whenToUse: As the raw landing zone / data lake for any GCP analytics stack.
Staging files that BigQuery loads or queries as external / BigLake tables.
Storing large immutable blobs: logs, exports, images, model artifacts, Parquet tables.
Cheap long-term retention with Nearline/Coldline/Archive and lifecycle rules.
Serving static assets, often fronted by Cloud CDN.
whenNotToUse: Low-latency random reads/writes of small records — use Bigtable or Firestore.
Data you need to update in place or transact over — objects are whole-file replace only.
A POSIX filesystem for lift-and-shift apps — use Filestore.
Structured data you'll mostly query with SQL — land it, but do the querying in BigQuery.

keyFacts.label: Durability
keyFacts.value: 11 nines (99.999999999%) annual durability, data redundantly stored.

keyFacts.label: Capacity
keyFacts.value: Unlimited objects and total size per bucket.

keyFacts.label: Consistency
keyFacts.value: Strong for object reads, writes and listing.

keyFacts.label: Scope
keyFacts.value: Bucket names are globally unique; data location is set per bucket.

pricingShape: You pay on: (1) storage per GB-month, much cheaper for colder classes but with minimum storage durations (delete a Coldline object early and you still pay the minimum); (2) operations — Class A (writes/lists) cost more than Class B (reads), so many tiny objects and heavy listing add up; (3) network egress — out to the internet or across regions is billed, while same-region reads to GCP services are cheap or free; and (4) retrieval fees on the colder classes. Co-locating the bucket with BigQuery and compute is the simplest way to keep the network bill near zero.
gotchas: Bucket names share one global namespace and hint that a bucket exists — avoid guessable names for sensitive data.
Cross-region and internet egress is billed; keep buckets in the same region as BigQuery and compute.
Colder classes have minimum storage durations and retrieval fees — churny data is cheaper in Standard.
Public access via 'allUsers' is the classic misconfig; prefer uniform bucket-level access and keep public off unless you mean it.
Querying files in place is convenient but pays per byte scanned in BigQuery — Parquet + partitioning still matters.

equivalents.name: Amazon S3
equivalents.note: The original object store; near 1:1 concepts (buckets, keys, storage classes).

equivalents.name: ADLS Gen2
equivalents.note: Blob storage with a true hierarchical namespace, so it behaves more folder-like than GCS.
